units: a resin put on the hair makes it grip more strongly
the hair drags the string and releases it over and over
that repetition produces a steady oscillation
the speed of the oscillation settles the note that is heard
a string on its own sets too little air moving
the vibration travels through a piece standing on the body
the body of the instrument starts moving in its turn
widening the vibrating surface makes the sound louder
text: Draw a bow across a taut string and the sound begins with a grip so small that no ear can catch it. The hair carries a dusting of resin, which leaves it faintly tacky. So the hair takes hold of the string, drags it a fraction to one side, then lets go all at once. The string springs back towards its resting place, the hair catches it again, and the cycle runs on without a break. Out of that catching and slipping comes a steady vibration, and how fast it runs decides the pitch we hear. On its own the string shifts far too little air to be heard across a room. It hands its movement instead to the bridge, a slim upright of wood standing on the belly of the instrument. The bridge sets that broad panel swinging, and the panel drives a great deal more air. The tone grows full because the vibrating surface has been made wider.

units: the head of the percussion instrument sounded dull late in the rehearsal
the conductor halts the rehearsal and sends for the repairer
dry air had shrunk the animal skin
tightening the fittings would have made matters worse
the repairer chooses to put moisture back into the room
vessels full of water are set out around the platform
the players carry on rehearsing in another room
with the give restored a slight adjustment brings the pitch back
text: The rehearsal was nearly over when the timpanist noticed that her drum had stopped answering her. Under the stick the head gave back a flat knock with no depth to it, as though every trace of tension had drained out of it. The conductor stopped the players and sent for the craftsman who looked after the instruments. He found the cause soon enough: weeks of very dry air in the hall had shrunk the natural skin stretched over the copper bowl. Turning the screws down would only have deepened the imbalance, and might well have torn the head across. He put forward something gentler, damping the air by degrees and letting the skin ease itself back. Wide basins of water were set out around the platform, and the players moved to another room to finish. By morning the head had recovered its give, and two turns of the key put the pitch right.

units: two blades must be examined before either is fitted
the soft blade bends under the pressure of a finger
the stiff blade keeps its shape when pressed
the blades have to be wetted before fitting
the fastening must not be closed too tightly
a low note is tried and then the same note high up
the soft blade speaks quickly but weakens in the top register
the stiff blade asks for more effort and stands up to loud playing
the choice rests on the tiredness felt after a long held sound
text: Lay two reeds side by side and look at both before you fit either one to the mouthpiece. The softer blade gives way under your thumb; the harder one pushes back and keeps its curve. Each suits a different job, and trying them beats trusting what you have been told. Wet both in a little warm water, then seat the first on the table of the mouthpiece and close the ligature without forcing it. Blow a long note low down, then the same note up in the top register. The soft reed speaks at once and sounds sweet, yet the high end slips away from you as soon as you press harder. The hard reed wants more support to start, gives a thicker tone and holds together when you play out. Keep whichever leaves you less tired after a long held note, not the one that charms you straight away.

units: the place where the instruments are made has lately opened to visitors
a smell of glue and cut wood meets you at the door
the space is divided into four working areas
the first area is for splitting and joining the boards
a student there shapes a part by hand without any powered tool
the finishing area is kept clear of moving air
each coat of finish dries before the next is put on
the last area allows the instrument to be tried by playing it
the person in charge says nothing leaves without being tested
one and the same wood yields instruments that sound different
text: Hot glue and freshly planed wood: that is what meets you the moment you step through the door of the workshop, which has only lately been opened to the public. Four benches share the hall. At the back sits the cutting, where boards of maple are split, turned over and glued up to form the backs. Over on the right, the fitting, where a young apprentice trims a bridge with a knife and never goes near a machine. Further along lies the varnishing room, held well clear of any draught, where a coat has to dry before the next goes on. The last bench, the busiest of the four, is for trying things out: strings go on, a bow is drawn, everyone listens. The man in charge warns visitors that nothing leaves the place unplayed. Most go away with a thought they had not expected, since two instruments cut from one board never sound alike.

units: the space is deserted late in the day before the session
the technical team lay the cables and hang two pickups
the players settle in and put their instruments in tune
the first take starts once night has come
one player fits an accessory that softens the tone
the person in charge of sound answers by moving a pickup back
stray noises can be heard during the pauses
the last take is the best one in spite of the exhaustion
the gear is packed away before the sun rises
text: Late in the afternoon the hall stands empty and the quiet inside it feels thick enough to touch. The technicians come in first, running their cables along the foot of the walls and hanging two microphones above the platform. The players drift in afterwards in twos and threes, settle without hurry and tune up in a peaceable sort of muddle. The first take begins after dark. A cellist clips a mute onto his bridge to soften the tone, and the engineer answers by drawing one microphone back. Between takes you catch the rustle of pages, a cough, a chair creaking under somebody who has shifted. Around midnight the tiredness shows in every face, and yet the take that holds together best is the last of them. The cables are coiled before the sun is up, and the hall goes back to its silence, a shade warmer than it was on arrival.

units: the absence of noise is now sold as a product
the humming of machines pushes the ear to sort very early
that protection of the hearing costs it its fineness
attention goes to masses of sound rather than to details
recorded sound is now made to survive the noise around it
such recordings in their turn deepen the listener's inattention
the writer describes a circle that feeds itself
bringing back the absence of noise is not a longing for the past
text: Quiet has turned into something we buy, and the change is worth pausing over. Machines hum on every side, so the ear learns early to sift, to push the murmur into the background and to expect nothing at all from what it takes in. That defence carries a price. Guarding itself season after season, our listening coarsens: it tells shades apart less well and settles for broad blocks of sound. What follows is music built to survive noise, squeezed and levelled, cut for the half attention of someone walking down a corridor. And since that music then fills the air everywhere, it trains the ear to attend less still, so the loop closes on itself. Giving quiet its place back has nothing to do with longing for what is gone; it is what lets sound become an event again, rather than a backdrop nobody notices.

units: the specialist opens the instrument before doing anything else
the middle register gives out a sound that is too harsh
she checks the tuning by working on the fittings of the strings
the trouble is still there after that check
the padding of the striking parts has packed down with use
grooves have been worn into it by the contact of the strings
she refuses to change the parts and would rather restore them
she pricks the padding with points to give it back its give
she then sets the control worked by the left foot
text: Before she lays a finger on the keys, the tuner lifts off the front panel and studies the works in silence. The instrument handed to her rings hard through the middle, as though every note there were being struck too bluntly. She goes over the tuning first, string by string, with a key that turns each pin an eighth of a turn. The fault stays where it is. So she looks at the hammers and finds her answer: the felt has packed down with use, gone hard, and carries grooves worn into it by the strings. Her remedy is not to swap the parts out but to nurse them. She pricks the felt of every hammer with fine needles to give it back its spring, then smooths the surface down. Last of all she sets the left pedal, which brings the hammers nearer the strings, and plays the middle again: the roundness is back.

units: two recordings of the same work for strings are set against each other
the older recording was made in a space of great size
the resonances pile up there and soften the starts of the notes
the listener has the feeling of sitting far away
the other recording was made with the pickups very close in
every group of instruments can be told apart in it
that precision costs the sense of space
neither of the two versions is called the better one
the distant recording suits the calm passages
the close recording suits the swift passages
text: Set two recordings of one and the same score for strings against each other, and you learn more than any quarrel about taste would ever teach you. The first, taken in a wide hall, lets the resonances run into one another; the attacks come out rounded, the edges a little blurred, and you seem to be hearing the players from the far end of the building. The second, made with the microphones brought up close, lays every desk bare: you catch the scrape of the bows, the breathing, the grain of the low strings. Such sharpness costs something, for the whole loses the depth that gave the other version its breadth. Neither of them carries the day outright. The distant balance convinces in the slow movements, while the close one takes over in quick passages, where clear drawing settles everything.

units: the writer answers a request for news about his learning
the first sessions went on holding the instrument without making a sound
that early constraint spared his shoulders
the teacher asks for a breath that comes from the belly
an uneven breath makes the note waver
the fingers grow nimble on their own once the groundwork holds
hearing is the faculty that takes longest to form
the writer now catches his own faults of tuning before they are pointed out
he asks the person he writes to come and listen the following week
text: You asked me how the lessons were going, so here is what a whole season of them has left me with. Posture came first: for weeks on end I held the instrument without sounding a single note, which struck me as daft at the time and which has saved my shoulders ever since. Then the breath. My teacher insists that the air must set off from the belly and reach the mouthpiece even, or else the note wobbles and dies on you. The fingers come third, and they look after themselves well enough as soon as the other two hold up. The ear is the slowest of the lot to ripen: I am beginning to hear that I am out of tune before anyone tells me so, and that heartens me rather more than it may sound. Come round next week, bring your own instrument if you like, and judge the results for yourself.

units: she began with cleaning and tidying jobs
she was not allowed near the mixing gear during her first year
she was then given the placing of the pickups on the percussion
an accessory badly fitted on a brass instrument can spoil a take
the hardest part was keeping her remarks to herself
she ran a session on her own to cover for an absent colleague
that successful session put an end to the lowly jobs
she now teaches the trade to newcomers
her chief instruction is to trust the ear and not the eye
text: First they ask her where it all began for her. She says she swept the studio floor and coiled the cables, carried the cases of gear about, and went a whole year without once laying a hand on the desk. And after that? After that they let her place the microphones on the drums, then on the brass, where a mute sitting wrong can ruin an entire take. The hardest part of those early days? Holding her tongue when she heard a fault that everybody else was letting through. In the end she ran the desk on her own one night, standing in for a colleague who had fallen ill; the session went off well, and nobody ever handed her a broom again after that. And now? Now she trains beginners, and drills into them the one rule she trusts: you place a microphone with your ears, never with your eyes.
